name: JsonFusion
workload: Six realistic parse+validate+populate scenarios (embedded config static/dynamic, telemetry samples, RPC commands, log events, bus events, metrics/time-series), 1M iterations each; separately, twitter.json (0.6 MB, 100 status objects) parse+populate+validate benchmark comparing full C++ library workflows.
claimed_speedup: vs RapidJSON+manual mapping: ~same speed on static embedded config, 40% faster dynamic embedded config, 20% faster telemetry, 65% faster RPC commands, 15% faster log events, 20% faster bus events, 15% faster metrics; ~1.5x faster on twitter.json (1020 microseconds/iter vs 1620 microseconds/iter). On canada.json (2.15MB) streaming with selective field-skipping, ~60% faster than hand-written RapidJSON SAX.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14 (6-scenario benchmark, optimization flags not stated); GCC 14.3 (twitter.json benchmark, flags not stated)
hardware: Apple M1 Max, macOS 26.1 (6-scenario benchmark); arm64 Ubuntu Linux 24.04 machine, CPU model not stated (twitter.json and canada.json benchmarks)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++23 reflection-based parser (uses Boost.PFR); no SIMD, no hand-tuned assembly by design; forward-only-iterator streaming API differs from DOM-based RapidJSON; default floating-point backend does not guarantee perfect round-trip precision; ~3x slower than Glaze and ~15% slower than RapidJSON on canada.json parse-and-populate; on 8-bit AVR its code size (25.8KB) is larger than jsmn/cJSON.
caveats: First-party README benchmark; CPU model given for one table (M1 Max) but compiler optimization flags are not stated for either table, so methodology is only partially specified; very young, low-star project just added to vcpkg; numbers are self-reported and not independently reproduced.
found_via: vcpkg ports directory scan for json-related ports (git tree of microsoft/vcpkg master, ports/jsonfusion/vcpkg.json) -> https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/tree/master/ports/jsonfusion

name: cpp-yyjson
workload: Read (parse a document and visit every element) and write (serialize a parsed document back to text) across ten JSON documents (0.1-66.4 MB, number-heavy to string-heavy) from the yyjson_benchmark dataset, measured with Google Benchmark (median of 11-101 repetitions, one process per run).
claimed_speedup: vs RapidJSON: 1.4-4.6x faster reads, 2.6-8.1x faster writes across the ten documents; time-weighted totals across the dataset: 2.31x faster reads, 3.91x faster writes. Also quantified vs simdjson (1.1-1.6x faster reads, weighted 2.14x; simdjson has no serializer), vs nlohmann-json (2.8-27x faster writes, weighted 6.67x; not compared for reads), and vs upstream yyjson (1.0-1.8x faster reads / 1.0-2.1x faster writes, weighted 1.69x/1.46x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15.2.0; all four benchmark executables built with -O3, -march=x86-64-v3 and link-time optimization (rapidjson and nlohmann-json are header-only and compiled with identical flags; simdjson and yyjson are prebuilt vcpkg libraries built without -march=x86-64-v3 or LTO).
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 8 logical CPUs (E-cores and Turbo Boost disabled), Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, Linux 7.0.0
tradeoffs: Requires a C++20 compiler with range support; bundled backend compiles yyjson.c from source (an external-yyjson mode is also available); the huge-page allocator optimization only applies on Linux/glibc for blocks >=32MB, so most of the weighted-average gain against yyjson/simdjson on the two largest documents (fgo, otfcc) comes from that platform-specific effect rather than parsing algorithm differences; simdjson has no serializer so is excluded from write comparisons and nlohmann-json is excluded from read comparisons.
caveats: The project's own README explicitly flags an asymmetry as the main caveat of its own comparison: simdjson and yyjson are linked as prebuilt vcpkg libraries without -march=x86-64-v3 or LTO, while header-only rapidjson and nlohmann-json get exactly the same optimization flags as cpp-yyjson itself -- this could inflate the margin against simdjson/yyjson specifically. Despite this self-disclosed asymmetry, compiler, flags, and hardware are all stated and benchmark code/raw logs are public, so it still meets Tier A's bar.
